title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Of these two peoples, then, Croesus was informed that the Athenian was held in subjection and torn by faction under Peisistratus, son of Hippocrates, who was at that time tyrant of the Athenians. For to Hippocrates, while he was still a private citizen and had gone to view the Olympic games, a great marvel had occurred. After he had offered the sacrifice, the cauldrons standing upon the hearth, full of pieces of flesh and of water, boiled over without fire beneath them and ran over. Chilon the Lacedaemonian, who happened to be present and to have seen the marvel, advised Hippocrates first not to bring into his house a wife to bear him children, and secondly, if he already had one, to dismiss her, and, if he happened to have a son, to disown him. But Hippocrates, they say, was not willing to be persuaded by Chilon’s advice. And so afterward this Peisistratus was born to him. When the Athenians of the shore were at feud with those of the plain—Megacles, son of Alcmaeon, being leader of the first faction, and Lycurgus, son of Aristolaidas, leader of that of the plain—Peisistratus aimed at the tyranny for himself and gathered a third party. After he had collected supporters and proclaimed himself leader of the men of the mountain-lands, he contrived the following device: he inflicted wounds upon himself and upon his mules, and then drove his chariot into the market-place as if he had just escaped from his enemies, who, he alleged, had tried to kill him as he was driving into the country. He then begged of the commons that he might obtain some protection from them, for before this he had gained a reputation in his command against the Megarians, during which he took Nisaea and performed other signal services. The commons of the Athenians, being deceived, gave him a body of men chosen from among the dwellers in the city—men who became not the spearmen of Peisistratus but his club-men, for they followed behind him bearing wooden clubs. These rose up with Peisistratus and seized the Acropolis. Then Peisistratus became ruler of the Athenians, without disturbing the existing magistrates or changing the ancient laws; but he administered the State under that constitution which was already established, ordering it fairly and well.
